sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Soft robotic gloves (SRGs) integrated with brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have demonstrated potential in facilitating motor recovery after stroke by enabling active, intention-driven rehabilitation. Emerging evidence suggests that incorporating vibrotactile stimulation (VTS) into SRG-BCI systems may further enhance sensorimotor feedback. The objective of this study is to evaluate the therapeutic efficacy and underlying neural mechanisms of BCI-driven, intention-based glove activation compared with automated glove-assisted training, with VTS applied identically in both groups.

sec.title: Methods and analysis
sec.p: This multicentre, single-blind, randomised controlled trial will involve 48 post-stroke patients within 1 week to 3 months after stroke onset, with stratification by time since stroke during randomisation. Participants will be randomly assigned to either the BCI-SRG group (n=24) or SRG group (n=24). Both groups will receive identical VTS. Patients in the BCI-SRG group will actively initiate movements of the SRG through motor imagery, while those in the SRG group will receive automated glove-assisted training without BCI control. The intervention will be administered 5 days per week for 4 weeks. The primary outcome measure is the Fugl-Meyer Assessment of Upper Extremity. Secondary outcome measures include Wolf Motor Function Test, International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health Generic Set, Barthel Index, Modified Ashworth Scale, Semmes-Weinstein Monofilament Test, as well as event-related spectral perturbation and event-related desynchronisation. All assessments will be conducted at both baseline and post-intervention.

sec.title: Ethics and dissemination
sec.p: Ethics approval of this study protocol has been obtained from the Ethics Committee of the First Affiliated Hospital with Nanjing Medical University (2025-SR-508). The findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed journals, conference presentations and communication with scientific, professional and general public audiences.

caption.title: STRENGTHS AND LIMITATIONS OF THIS STUDY

list-item.p: This study will be a multicentre, single-blind, randomised controlled trial.

EEG data will be recorded continuously during each session in the brain-computer interfaces (BCI)-soft robotic glove (SRG) group, while in the SRG group EEG will be collected at baseline and post-intervention, enabling between-group comparisons of cortical activation patterns and recovery mechanisms.
Both quantitative and qualitative outcome measures will be collected.
Standardised protocols will be applied across all study sites to ensure consistency.

The absence of a sham-BCI condition may introduce potential attention or motivation bias, although an active SRG-based comparator will be used to control for non-specific effects of device-assisted rehabilitation.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Stroke is a cerebrovascular disorder characterised by the sudden interruption of cerebral blood flow, typically due to vascular occlusion or rupture.1 According to the Global Burden of Disease Study, stroke affected 12.2 million people and resulted in 6.55 million deaths worldwide in 2019, ranking as the third leading cause of disability-adjusted life years globally.2 Upper limb motor impairment is one of the most common and disabling consequences of stroke. Approximately 80% of stroke survivors fail to fully regain upper limb function, which limits daily activities, reduces quality of life and leads to a loss of independence.3 Accordingly, restoration of upper limb function has emerged as the primary therapeutic goal in post-stroke rehabilitation.4 However, these approaches often lack adequate patient-initiated engagement and fail to deliver task-specific training. Thus, such limitations may impede the effective activation of neuroplastic mechanisms that are critical for motor relearning and functional recovery. To overcome these challenges, there is a growing need for more effective rehabilitation strategies to enhance upper limb motor function in stroke patients.

Soft robotic gloves (SRGs) have shown potential in facilitating motor recovery in neurorehabilitation. The gloves employ lightweight, flexible actuators, such as textiles or pneumatics, to assist repetitive, task-specific finger and hand movements that closely mimic natural motion.5 Compared with rigid exoskeletal systems, SRGs offer greater safety, comfort and adaptability, making them particularly suitable for clinical rehabilitation. In addition to mechanical assistance, robotic gloves contribute to motor relearning by reinforcing sensorimotor pathways that are essential for neuroplasticity.6 Previous studies have demonstrated the efficacy of SRGs in enhancing motor function. For example, Shi et al7 observed significant improvements in grip strength among chronic stroke patients after 20 sessions of soft glove-assisted training. Similarly, Wang et al8 reported that SRG-assisted therapy effectively promotes neuroplastic changes through enhanced sensorimotor stimulation and repetitive activation of the affected limb. This sensory feedback supports the formation of new synapses, dendritic growth and cortical remodelling following focal injury. However, the overall effectiveness of SRGs remains uncertain. While several studies have reported functional improvements, others have shown limited or no significant benefits.9 This variability may stem from the fact that most SRG interventions rely on passive movement, which insufficiently engages voluntary motor control and cortical activation.10 These findings highlight the need to further optimise SRG-based rehabilitation by incorporating strategies that promote active participation and stimulate neuroplastic changes more effectively.

Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have evolved as a transformative neurorehabilitation approach that bridges neural activity with assistive devices. They enable direct communication between the brain and external devices by decoding motor intentions from brain signals such as the electroencephalography (EEG).11 A typical BCI system includes several components: EEG signal acquisition, preprocessing, feature extraction, classification and control of external devices. Among various BCI paradigms, motor imagery-based BCI (MI-BCI), which involves the mental simulation of movement without physical execution, has been widely used as an intervention for post-stroke rehabilitation. MI evokes cortical activity patterns analogous to those generated during actual movement, thereby activating sensorimotor pathways involved in motor relearning.12 This mechanism aligns with the principle of neuroplasticity, in which repeated MI induces reorganisation of brain functional networks, thereby enhancing coordination among motor-related, sensory and associative cortical regions. Such reorganisation supports motor relearning and contributes to functional recovery in post-stroke patients.13 Recent studies have demonstrated that integrating BCI systems with robotic devices14 or functional electrical stimulation15 can create a closed-loop rehabilitation system that enables bidirectional interaction between cortical activation and sensory feedback. For instance, a randomised controlled study demonstrated that BCI-controlled SRG significantly improved upper limb motor function in subacute stroke patients, with cortical activation changes suggesting functional reorganisation of motor-related brain regions.16

Although MI-BCI systems show promise in promoting motor recovery, their efficacy remains highly dependent on user engagement and the quality of sensory feedback. To further enhance the effectiveness of MI-BCI systems, recent research has explored the integration of vibrotactile stimulation (VTS) with MI-BCI systems. Existing studies have indicated that VTS modulates sensorimotor rhythms by enhancing event-related desynchronisation (ERD) in alpha and beta bands,17 18 thereby facilitating MI execution and reducing the rate of BCI illiteracy.1921 Stronger ERD indicates greater activation of the motor cortex, which is essential for effective BCI control and for promoting neuroplastic changes. Furthermore, VTS has been shown to increase EEG classification accuracy22 and reduce calibration time in the somatosensory BCI system.23 Moreover, recent evidence suggests that VTS accelerates cortical activation dynamics, particularly enhancing the responsiveness of brain regions involved in tactile processing. This enhancement is accompanied by increased activation in the contralateral motor cortex during MI of the non-dominant hand. Such neurophysiological modulation contributes to improved online decoding accuracy of MI tasks and strengthens the robustness and reliability of the BCI control system.24 Collectively, these findings further support the integration of vibrotactile feedback as a valuable approach to optimise MI-BCI performance and promote more effective neurorehabilitation outcomes. In this study, VTS will be incorporated as a supportive and standardised component of the rehabilitation system, rather than as an independent experimental variable, thereby enabling the isolation of the therapeutic effects attributable to BCI-driven glove control.

The combination of MI-BCI, SRG assistance and VTS represents a comprehensive approach to upper limb rehabilitation. In this multimodal system, the BCI detects motor intention and activates the SRG to perform the corresponding hand movements. Simultaneously, VTS provides sensory feedback to the hand, which can reinforce the perception of movement and promote better integration of sensory and motor signals. This integrative approach not only delivers personalised physical support but also enhances mental engagement through MI, thereby activating multiple pathways of recovery. However, there is a lack of systematic studies evaluating the efficacy of integrating MI-BCI, SRG and VTS into a unified neurorehabilitation approach. This study aims to investigate whether BCI-driven SRG training can more effectively improve upper limb function and promote neuroplasticity in post-stroke patients compared with automated glove-assisted therapy without BCI involvement. By combining motor intention decoding, sensorimotor stimulation and task-specific physical assistance, this multimodal intervention is expected to promote greater patient engagement and yield superior functional outcomes. It is anticipated that this approach will contribute to the development of personalised, mechanism-based rehabilitation paradigms for stroke recovery.

sec.title: Methods and analysis
sec.p: This study will be a multicentre, single-blind, randomised controlled trial with two groups: the BCI-SRG and the SRG group.

sec.title: Study setting
sec.p: The study will be conducted over a 12-month period, from 1 August 2025 to 1 August 2026. Participants will be recruited from three clinical sites: the First Affiliated Hospital with Nanjing Medical University, Kunshan Rehabilitation Hospital and the First Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-sen University. These centres specialise in inpatient rehabilitation and have extensive expertise in managing post-stroke patients. All study procedures, including screening, informed consent, intervention delivery and outcome assessments will be conducted at these sites by trained personnel in accordance with standardised protocols.

sec.title: Patient and public involvement
sec.p: Patient and public involvement (PPI) representatives will actively participate in the design and management of this study to enhance clinical relevance and feasibility. During the design stage, PPI representatives will contribute to refining the research objectives and ensuring alignment with patient priorities. Their feedback will be sought on eligibility criteria, recruitment strategies and participant information materials to minimise burden and improve accessibility. They will also provide guidance on the acceptability of intervention procedures and offer input on study management where appropriate.

sec.title: Recruitment and screening
sec.p: Patients will be recruited from the neurological rehabilitation departments of three subcentres. Trained research staff, including rehabilitation specialists, clinical research coordinators and physicians, will identify eligible candidates through hospital admission records and will screen them according to predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. Prior to enrolment, detailed information about the study’s objectives, procedures, potential risks and expected benefits will be provided to ensure participants’ full understanding. Each participant will be required to provide written informed consent before participating in any procedures related to the study. Following consent, participants will be randomly allocated in a 1:1 ratio to either the BCI-SRG group or the SRG group. To enhance adherence, the study team will conduct pre-trial education, clearly define individual responsibilities and proactively address potential barriers, thereby promoting patient compliance. Standardised checklists will be employed to monitor participant involvement and to promptly follow-up on any missed sessions or interventions.

sec.title: Inclusion criteria
sec.p: The inclusion criteria will be as follows: (1) cerebral haemorrhage and cerebral infarction confirmed by CT and/or MRI; (2) first-ever or unilateral stroke, or a history of stroke without residual neurological deficits; (3) stable vital signs; (4) age between 40 and 75 years; (5) stroke onset within 1 week to 3 months; (6) Brunnstrom stage I–IV for the affected upper limb; (7) Mini-Mental State Examination score >20; (8) written informed consent obtained from the patient or their legal guardian.

sec.title: Exclusion criteria
sec.p: The exclusion criteria will be as follows: (1) severe muscle spasticity with Modified Ashworth Scale (MAS) >2; (2) visual impairments; (3) posterior circulation stroke; (4) severe cardiopulmonary disease or multi-organ failure; (5) pregnancy; (6) other musculoskeletal disorders or significant joint pain in the hemiparetic upper limb; (7) other neurological disorders, such as brain tumours, psychiatric disorders or Parkinson’s disease.

sec.title: Sample size
sec.p: The sample size was determined using G*Power V.3.9.1.2 software based on an independent t-test to evaluate the effectiveness of BCI combined with SRG-VTS training on upper limb functional recovery in stroke patients. The FMA-UE was selected as the primary outcome measure for estimating the required sample size. Based on the previous study conducted by Choi et al,25 a large expected effect size (Cohen’s d ≈ 0.87) was assumed for the power analysis. This effect size was calculated based on the between-group difference in post-intervention FMA-UE scores in that study. In addition, evidence from prior studies indicates that a between-group difference of approximately 13 points on the FMA-UE represents a clinically meaningful superiority margin for upper limb motor recovery after stroke.26 Using a two-sided alpha level of 0.05 and a statistical power of 0.80, the required sample size was estimated at 22 participants per group. Considering a 10% dropout rate, a total of 48 participants will be enrolled, with 24 participants in each group.

sec.title: Randomisation and blinding
sec.p: After completion of baseline assessments and confirmation of eligibility based on the inclusion and exclusion criteria, participants will be randomly assigned to two groups: the BCI-SRG group and the SRG group, using a stratified block randomisation scheme. A trial statistician will generate the random sequence using the randomly permuted blocks with a size of 4 or 6 per block. Stratified blocked randomisation will be used to equalise the predictive factors across groups, including gender, stroke type, age and time since stroke onset. Time since stroke onset will be stratified into early subacute (1–6 weeks) and late subacute (7–12 weeks) phases prior to randomisation to ensure a balanced distribution of participants at different recovery stages between the two groups. To ensure blinding, group assignments will be sealed in opaque envelopes and will be stored in a secure cabinet. Participants will remain blinded to their group assignment until the envelope is opened. Evaluator blinding will be maintained throughout the study to reduce the risk of assessment bias. An independent research coordinator will monitor the randomisation process in order to maintain protocol compliance for each subject. Participants’ confidentiality will be strictly preserved by using identification numbers or Arabic numerals instead of personal information. Group allocations will be concealed from outcome assessors, data managers and statisticians until the final data analysis is completed. To minimise potential attention- or motivation-related bias between the two groups, both groups will undergo an identical number of glove-assisted grasp-and-extension training sessions under the same training conditions, with a therapist present throughout each session to ensure protocol adherence and maintain participant engagement. Participants will be informed that both interventions represent advanced forms of glove-assisted rehabilitation, without emphasising the superiority of the BCI component. If a severe adverse event or unexpected response occurs during the trial, unblinding may be required to provide appropriate clinical management. This decision must be approved by the investigator or physician and documented in the protocol to reduce bias and ensure data quality. Subsequently, these incidents will be submitted to the Ethical Committees of the primary hospital involved (figure 1).

sec.title: Intervention
sec.p: Patients will be randomly assigned to either the BCI-SRG or the SRG group. Both groups will participate in a 4-week rehabilitation programme that includes conventional physical therapy and occupational therapy, such as stretching, joint range-of-motion exercises, fine motor training and others. In addition to standard rehabilitation, the BCI-SRG group will receive BCI-SRG-based training, whereas the SRG group will receive SRG-based training alone. VTS will be delivered to both groups using identical parameters. This intervention will be administered once daily, 5 days per week, over the 4-week intervention period, resulting in a total of 20 sessions. Any adverse events occurring during the intervention period will be closely monitored and recorded. The timeline and structure of the intervention are illustrated in figure 2.

sec.title: EEG acquisition and neural mechanism analysis
sec.p: A 64-channel Okti EEG system (Compumedics, USA) will be used to collect EEG data. Electrodes will be positioned according to the International 10–20 system to ensure comprehensive coverage of major cortical regions, including the frontal, central, parietal, temporal and occipital lobes. The FCz electrode will serve as the reference, while the FPz electrode will serve as the ground to minimise environmental artefacts. The sampling rate will be set at 1000 Hz, and electrode impedance will be maintained below 15 kΩ to ensure high-quality signal acquisition. To improve signal clarity, the signal will be processed using a bandpass filter ranging from 0.1 to 100 Hz, along with a 50 Hz notch filter to attenuate signal interference.

In the BCI-SRG group, real-time EEG signal classification will be performed using a lightweight Interactive Frequency Convolutional Neural Network,27 which is initially pretrained on MI data from healthy subjects (OpenBMI dataset). Throughout the experimental sessions, the network will be incrementally fine-tuned and adaptively updated using subject-specific training data and daily acquired online MI data. This process aims to enhance individual decoding accuracy, improve classification performance and ensure personalised adaptation to each participant’s neural patterns.

To investigate the neural mechanism underlying motor recovery, ERD in the sensorimotor mu (8–12 Hz) and beta (13–30 Hz) frequency bands will be analysed during MI and glove-assisted movement tasks, as these frequency bands are closely associated with sensorimotor cortical activation and motor intention processing. Regions of interest will be defined over the bilateral sensorimotor cortices corresponding to electrodes C3 and C4 of the International 10–20 system, with hemisphere assignment adjusted according to the affected limb such that the contralateral hemisphere will represent the lesioned side and the ipsilateral hemisphere will represent the non-lesioned side. To quantitatively characterise hemispheric activation balance, an ERD-based lateralisation index (LI) will be calculated as follows:

where ERDcontralateral and ERDipsilateral denote the mean ERD values over the contralateral and ipsilateral sensorimotor cortices, respectively. The LI ranges from −1 to +1, where positive values will indicate dominant contralateral sensorimotor activation and negative values will indicate dominant ipsilateral activation. A post-intervention increase in positive LI values will be interpreted as a shift towards restored physiological lateralisation, reflecting true neurological recovery, whereas functional improvement accompanied by persistent or increased ipsilateral ERD will be interpreted as functional compensation via recruitment of homologous sensorimotor regions. Within-group pre-post changes in ERD power and LI will be analysed, between-group differences in LI changes will be compared, and correlation analyses will be conducted to examine the relationship between EEG-derived neural metrics and improvements in clinical motor outcomes.

sec.title: Soft rehabilitation glove and vibrotactile stimulation
sec.p: In this study, we will use a pneumatic soft glove, developed by the Laboratory of the School of Instrument Science and Engineering at Southeast University.28 The glove is equipped with a fabric-based, dual-layer pneumatic actuator with a honeycomb structure, which facilitates both finger flexion and extension to assist movement in the affected hand of stroke patients. Our previous studies have shown that the glove significantly increases finger mobility, improves fingertip force and enhances the functional movement of the fingers during activities of daily living.29

To further enhance motor recovery, VTS will be integrated to enhance sensory input during training. VTS will be applied identically in both the BCI-SRG and SRG groups, serving as a constant component of the intervention rather than an independent experimental variable. In particular, two lateral linear vibration actuators (ELV0632, AAC, China), each measuring 10 mm in diameter and 2 mm in thickness, will be affixed to the anterior and posterior sides of the patient’s wrist using medical tape. VTS will be applied during the MI phase for the BCI group and during glove-assisted passive rehabilitation training phase for both groups. At the beginning of the MI phase, both actuators will vibrate simultaneously at a frequency of 100 Hz for 2 s to help participants focus on the imagery task. During passive rehabilitation, the actuator on the anterior wrist will vibrate at 180 Hz during grasping movements, while the actuator on the posterior wrist will vibrate at 180 Hz during extension movements, thereby enhancing proprioceptive feedback. Prior to the intervention, all patients undergo a preliminary vibration intensity perception test to determine a stimulation level that is clearly perceptible without interfering with MI performance.

sec.title: Experimental procedure
sec.p: Patients in both the BCI-SRG and SRG groups will receive training that combines SRG with VTS. EEG signals will be continuously recorded throughout the intervention in the BCI-SRG group, while EEG data will be collected only during the initial and final sessions for the SRG group. In the BCI-SRG group, glove-assisted movements are actively initiated by patients’ motor intention, whereas in the SRG group, hand movements are passively initiated by the glove without voluntary control. Throughout all training sessions, a therapist will be present for both groups to provide standardised guidance, ensure task compliance and maintain patient engagement, thereby reducing differential attention effects between groups.

During training sessions, patients will be seated comfortably at a distance of approximately 1.5 metres from the display screen. The affected hand will be fitted with the robotic glove and placed in a relaxed, palm-up position on an armrest, ensuring that no external objects interfere with the robotic glove.

Treatment will be administered 5 days per week, with each day comprising three runs of 20 trials. The timeline for each trial is illustrated in figure 3. Prior to the intervention, patients in the BCI-SRG will undergo 1 to 2 days of MI training to familiarise themselves with the procedure and improve their ability to control the BCI system via mental imagery.

caption.title: Timeline for each trial. Both groups complete a total of 60 trials. The BCI-SRG group receives three runs of 20 trials each, while the SRG group completes all 60 trials in a single session. BCI, brain-computer interface; MI, motor imagery; SRG, soft robotic glove.

sec.p: In the BCI-SRG group, each trial begins with a 10 s resting-state period to establish a baseline, followed by a 5 s rest cue. A video is then displayed, showing a virtual hand corresponding to the patient’s affected side, prompting the patient to begin imagining the movement of their affected hand. At the same time, VTS will be delivered to the wrist to enhance sensory input. The MI phase lasts for 4 s and will be analysed using a sliding window approach, in which a 2 s window advances in 1 s increments, resulting in three classification results. Based on the classification outputs, the system determines whether the MI attempt is successful. On successful recognition of the patient’s MI, the SRG will be activated to assist the hand in executing the grasp-and-extension movement, which is sustained for 10 s. If no MI is detected within this period, the trial will be classified as unsuccessful and no robotic assistance will be provided. Subsequently, a failure message will be displayed on the screen for 3 s to inform the patient while encouraging them to maintain motivation and focus more intently in the following trial. The system then proceeds to the next trial.

In the SRG group, patients will undergo the same experimental procedure as those in the BCI-SRG group, with the exception that they do not engage in MI. During the intervention, the robotic glove will passively move the patient’s affected hand based on predefined parameters. Each cycle consists of a 10 s grasp-extension movement followed by a 5 s rest period. The training session lasts 15 min, during which 60 cycles of passive movement will be administered (figure 3).

sec.title: Outcome assessment
sec.p: In this study, demographic information and relevant clinical data, including age, sex, height, weight, stroke type and lesion location, will be collected from all participants at baseline. Both primary and secondary outcomes will be evaluated at baseline and at the end of the 4 week intervention.

sec.title: Primary outcome
sec.p: The Fugl-Meyer Assessment-Upper Extremity (FMA-UE)30 will serve as the primary outcome measure to assess the degree of functional recovery in the upper extremity following stroke. As the upper extremity assessment is the objective of this study, only the upper extremity section of the evaluation will be selected, with a total score of 66. Higher scores indicate better motor function and lower impairment.

sec.title: Secondary outcome
sec.p: The Wolf Motor Function Test (WMFT)31 is an upper extremity motor function test composed of 17 tasks: 15 functional movements and 2 strength assessments. The six-point Functional Ability Scale (FAS) describes functional ability for each task, while time is recorded separately for each task. Better motor control and functional recovery are represented by improvements in FAS scores.

The International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health Generic Set (ICF Generic Set)32 comprises 17 items representing main categories of body functions, activities and social participation. Each item is assessed for impairment severity using a standardised scale: 0 (no impairment), 1 (mild), 2 (moderate), 3 (severe) and 4 (complete impairment). A score of 8 indicates unquantifiable severity due to insufficient information and 9 refers to items that were excluded from the assessment.

The Barthel Index (BI)33 contains 10 items, each scored according to the degree of assistance needed by the individual to perform daily activities. Each item receives an increasing score, typically 0, 5, 10 or 15 points. The total score ranges from 0 to 100, with higher scores representing higher levels of functioning.

The Modified Ashworth Scale (MAS)34 is one of the most widely used clinical tools for assessing spasticity in patients with upper motor neuron lesions. It is applied on a six-point ordinal scale: 0, 1, 1+, 2, 3, 4. The degree of spasticity is evaluated by muscle tone, with a score of 0 representing ‘no increase in muscle tone’ and a score of 4 representing ‘rigid limb in flexion or extension.’

The Semmes-Weinstein Monofilament Test (SWMT)35 uses a set of nylon monofilaments of different diameters, each calibrated to a specific force that causes the filament to bend when applied perpendicularly to the skin. Monofilaments with thicknesses of 2.83, 3.61, 4.31, 4.56 and 6.65 will then be applied at several anatomical sites, including thumb pulp, thenar eminence, index finger pulp, little finger pulp, hypothenar eminence, dorsal hand and wrist. Higher threshold values indicate greater sensory impairment.

Event-Related Spectral Perturbation (ERSP) and ERD36 are quantitative EEG data analysis techniques used to examine dynamic changes in brain oscillatory activity related to specific sensory, cognitive or motor events. ERSP will be used to characterise dynamic task-related increases and decreases in spectral power across frequency bands, whereas ERD will specifically quantify relative power reductions in the sensorimotor mu and beta rhythms, which are widely recognised as neurophysiological markers of motor cortical activation. Changes in ERD patterns following the intervention will be analysed to explore cortical reorganisation associated with MI and glove-assisted movement, thereby providing mechanistic insight into the neural reorganisation patterns associated with functional motor recovery.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: The primary analysis will be conducted based on the intention-to-treat principle, which includes all randomised patients. This method maintains the integrity of the randomisation process and provides an unbiased estimate of the treatment effect. Besides, a per-protocol analysis will be performed, including only those patients who strictly complied with the study protocol, received the assigned intervention and did not experience major protocol deviations. This analysis will help to evaluate the efficacy of the intervention under ideal compliance conditions.

To account for potential baseline heterogeneity associated with recovery stage, time since stroke onset will be included as a covariate in the primary outcome analysis. An analysis of covariance model will be applied to compare post-intervention FMA-UE scores between groups, with baseline FMA-UE score and time since stroke onset as covariates. This approach will allow adjustment for differences in neurological stability and spontaneous recovery associated with stroke chronicity.

Subgroup analyses will be performed based on baseline characteristics such as age, sex or disease severity. The decision to carry out these subgroup analyses will be made after reviewing the baseline data.

Quantitative data analyses will be conducted using the Shapiro-Wilk test implemented in SPSS V.23.0 by statisticians who are independent of this study. Continuous variables demonstrating a normal distribution will be expressed as mean±SD, while non-normally distributed measurements will be reported as median with IQR. Categorical variables will be described using frequency counts and percentages. For parametric continuous data, within-group pre-post intervention comparisons will use paired t-tests, whereas between-group analyses will use independent-sample t-tests. Non-parametric equivalents will apply Wilcoxon signed-rank tests for longitudinal comparisons. Between-group differences in categorical outcomes will be evaluated using chi-square tests, with all analyses conducted at a two-tailed significance threshold of p<0.05. Any missing primary outcome data will be addressed by referencing baseline assessments and conducting additional sensitivity analyses to assess the robustness of the results.

sec.title: Data collection, management and monitoring
sec.p: All baseline data will be collected and recorded accurately and clearly on Case Report Forms (CRFs) by physicians and therapists. Data will be cross-checked to ensure accuracy. All study documents will then be assigned a unique study identification number, digitised and entered into the dataset by research assistants. After verifying the accuracy and consistency of data, assistants will transfer verified paper records into an electronic database using Microsoft Excel spreadsheets. All paper and electronic data related to the study will be safely stored. Only those who are independent of the study will have access for data checking and auditing to ensure data security. All data will be securely stored for 5 years after study completion. In order to protect patient privacy, information that could be used to identify patient will not be disclosed in publications.

An independent Data Safety and Monitoring Committee, composed of experts in rehabilitation, neurology, ethics and statistics, will be established to ensure data confidentiality and protocol compliance. The committee will have no conflicts of interest and will be independent of this trial. They will monitor trial compliance by ensuring validation of data consistency, logic and accuracy through systematic reviews of collected data and cross-checking entries against predefined criteria. Besides, the Data Monitoring Committee will assess overall data completeness by interviewing investigators, auditing source documents and confirming alignment with the study protocol principles. In case of any abnormalities during the trial, they will communicate with relevant individuals to investigate and resolve the issues. These procedures aim to minimise data inaccuracies and systematic bias, thereby ensuring data integrity and supporting reliable data analysis.

sec.title: Quality control
sec.p: To ensure the quality of the study, an independent quality control team will be established. The team will oversee patient enrolment and disease assessment to minimise selection bias. It will also be responsible for patient education and ongoing communication throughout the study. These measures can help to enhance participant adherence and to reduce loss to follow-up.

sec.title: Safety assessment
sec.p: To minimise the risk of adverse effects, a comprehensive safety evaluation will be conducted throughout the study. All participants will first undergo a screening process based on predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. EEG testing is generally considered safe; however, some individuals may experience mild skin irritation at electrode sites, which typically resolves shortly after the procedure. In the event of any adverse incidents, such as signal decoding failures or unintended robotic movements, the research team will promptly investigate and resolve these events. If a participant’s condition deteriorates during the trial, the participant will be withdrawn from the study and provided with appropriate medical care at no cost. All adverse events will be thoroughly documented in the CRF. Furthermore, serious adverse events will be reported to the principal investigator and relevant regulatory authorities within 24 hours. This trial will be monitored by the Hospital Research Ethics Committee to ensure adherence to the study protocol and to implement necessary procedural adjustments when required.

sec.title: Research ethics approval
sec.p: The study protocol was reviewed and approved by the Ethics Committee of the First Affiliated Hospital with Nanjing Medical University (2025-SR-508).

sec.title: Protocol amendments
sec.p: Revisions to the protocol will only be made after comprehensive review and approval by the Hospital Research Ethics Committee. Once the amendments are approved and registered with the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry, the updated protocol will be implemented accordingly.

sec.title: Consent or assent
sec.p: To ensure proper ethical conduct and informed participation, the research team will conduct thorough pre-trial discussions with participants to clearly explain the study’s scientific rationale and procedures. This includes participants’ responsibilities, potential risks and benefits, possible side effects and the randomisation procedure of the study. Participants will be informed that participation is entirely voluntary and that they may withdraw from the study at any time, without any impact on their routine medical care. Written informed consent will be obtained after confirming the participant’s full understanding of the study and voluntary agreement to participate. These procedures are intended to ensure that ethical standards are maintained throughout the research process.
